title: Useless scum
body: “Privacy First” — until you read the documentation. When I tested the app, I discovered that moshi-hook was designed to send snippets of prompts, agent responses, approval commands, and project metadata to the developer’s servers. This deserves a clear warning during setup, not a documentation hunt followed by figuring out how to disable the data transfers yourself. I spent about five hours troubleshooting and trying to get the features I needed working with privacy settings I was comfortable with. I never got a usable setup. On top of that, the app drained my battery like crazy. I cancelled the subscription, and Apple explicitly shows it as cancelled. After that, attempts to charge me $9.99 started anyway. Some “trial”: hours wasted, a drained battery, privacy concerns, and then even more time needed to sort out billing after cancellation. The whole experience felt like a total scam. Not recommended.

title: thank goodness for Moshi
body: I was designing and doing mock-ups for my dream terminal application. It would present tmux and herdr sessions, panes, and windows. It would let me easily tail agent outputs and respond to requests. It would give me a familiar hands-on terminal for one-handed operation. I spent a couple of weeks playing with some ideas and did one last call before I started making commits and then💥: moshi entered that chat. For decades my primary interface to my computers is a terminal window. And this age of agentic systems rewards users like me, until we're in line at the market and Claude Code is requesting access to the 1password CLI to get an API credential. Almost everything I _dreamed_ of having was already in Moshi the day I installed it. Once I installed `moshi-hook` via macOS and linux homebrew on my essential workstations and servers at home, and the first agent notification from Claude and then another one from Hermes, when Hermes Agent wasn't even listed as a supported harness yet, I was right on time for Moshi. Seeing the agent activity cards and approving requests with a tap instead of scrunching my face at my phone looking over my glasses sent me running to the Yearly Subscription button and I'd do it again. This is the best terminal experience I've ever had on a mobile device, period. I've been using terminal multiplexers since the 1900s; GNU screen(1) was my gateway drug to let me leave an IRC bot online to take messages for me while I was offline. This isn't "ha look you can even ssh from this thing" this is "ha watch me redteam this application with a 12 agent fan-out with one command" and I'm never going back.

title: Where have you been all my life, Moshi?!
body: I spend a lot of time connecting to my home lab and cloud servers from my iPhone. I manage running containers, packages on the host, etc. Over the past 18 months, my usage has skyrocketed thanks to Claude Code, which allows me to make progress on my first-party apps and open source projects much more effectively than attempting to tap out code in NeoVim. I’ve been using Blink shell for years, but have never been very happy with it. The sole reason I’ve stuck with it comes down to one feature: proper handling of custom fonts with programming ligatures and NerdFont icons. I feel like I’ve tested dozens of apps and they either don’t handle ligatures or don’t have support for custom fonts at all. While Blink works, you have to go through a whole song and dance with uploading your font to a web server and writing a CSS file that embeds it. PITA. Enter Mochi! Not only does this app have support for custom fonts, you can add them directly from Files. No fiddling with CSS or web servers. The ligature support is perfect, and NerdFont icons render like a dream. Not only does Mochi pass the font test, it’s superior to Blink and every other terminal app I’ve tried, with awesome customization abilities, first class support for tmux, handy Claude Code features I never knew I needed, and intuitive management of sessions and favorite servers. I could go on and on. Five stars isn’t enough, frankly, so I’ve gone ahead and paid for a lifetime license, even though it will take years to make financial sense. I consider it a small price to pay up front to reward the developer for crafting such a wonderful app. Thank you!
